title: Four, five times
hook: Uttama left her cell again and again, restless, until the day she stayed (Therigatha, Uttama)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mutta, freed from mortar, pestle and crooked husband. Your line was so freed. Which freedom did you name? Day seven hundred eighty-five.

A door opens. A nun steps out of her small dwelling and stands there. She can't settle. She goes back in and sits. Before long she's on her feet and out again. The Therigatha doesn't hide this, and neither does she. In her own poem a nun named Uttama counts it: four times, five times, she went out of her dwelling, with no peace of mind and her thoughts out of her control. It's an honest number. Not once. Not a hundred. Four, five. Today, the number she remembered, and what came after it.
screen: `A DOOR OPENS.` → `OUT, AND BACK, AND OUT.` → `FOUR, FIVE TIMES.`

segments.voice: First, the leaving. Uttama's poem begins with restlessness, plainly told. She had gone forth. She had a place to sit. And she kept getting up. The restlessness wasn't something she'd outgrown before she joined. It came with her into the robe. Second, the help. Then, the poem says, she went to a nun she could trust. That nun taught her the dhamma: how a person is made of changing parts, the senses and their objects, the elements. Uttama didn't solve her restlessness alone in her room. She went and asked someone. Third, the sitting. Having heard the teaching, she did what she'd been asked. And the poem says she sat in one posture for seven days, steeped in joy and ease. Fourth, the darkness broken. On the eighth day, the poem says, she stretched out her legs, having torn through the mass of darkness. The same picture as Punna's poem: wisdom breaking the dark. So the shape of Uttama's poem is out, out, out, then help, then stillness. The four and five times aren't cut from the story to make her look better. They're the first line. The tradition kept the count of her leavings right beside the moment she came free, as if the leaving were part of the path that led to the staying. And the staying came after the help, not instead of the leaving.
screen: `OUT OF THE ROOM, AGAIN.` · `A NUN SHE COULD TRUST.` · `SHE SAT, AND STAYED.` · `THE DARKNESS BROKEN.` · then, large: `SHE STAYED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: return to the cushion once more. Settle, wherever you are; a chair works as well as a cushion. During the sit, the mind may leave. It may leave four times, five times, more. Each time you see it has gone, come back to the breath. Don't count the leaving as failure. Uttama's poem counts it plainly and goes on. Out, and back. Out, and back. The coming back is the practice. The bell holds the time.
Four. Four times, five times, Uttama left her dwelling without peace, until, with help, she sat and stayed. Today's word.
Your line: she stayed. Today, when you want to get up from something that matters, a task, a talk, a quiet minute, stay one minute longer. Day seven hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Some meditation teachers describe noticing the wandering mind and returning to the breath as the heart of sitting practice, and Uttama's verse is read as an honest account of restlessness on the way to stillness.

fork.setup: you're Uttama. four, five times you've left your dwelling, restless, your thoughts out of control. what do you do next?
options: give up the robe and go home.
go to a nun you trust and listen.
lock yourself in and try harder alone.
fork.reveal: she goes to a nun she trusts, hears the teaching, and then sits in one posture until the darkness breaks.

original.note: Pali catukkhattuṃ: four times. The opening word of Uttama's verse.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nun who couldn't sit still.
what it means: restlessness counted honestly, help asked for, and then she sat and stayed.
what a scholar hears: the commentary names the nun Uttama went to as Patacara; the verse itself says only that she went to a nun she could trust.
recall: takes the rules like a garland

sources.ref: Therigatha commentary on Uttama (the teacher named as Patacara)

notes: Thig 3.2 paraphrased: four or five times she left her dwelling without peace of mind, thoughts out of control; went to a trusted nun who taught her the aggregates, sense spheres and elements; sat in one posture for seven days steeped in rapture and ease; on the eighth stretched out her legs having torn apart the mass of darkness. Confirm all details, including the 'seven days' and 'eighth day' (stated only because the verse says them).
The teaching is rendered in plain words ('how a person is made of changing parts, the senses and their objects, the elements') for khandha, ayatana, dhatu; confirm.
Commentary identifying the teacher as Patacara: confirm (it links to tomorrow's day on Patacara).
Original: चतुक्खत्तुं (catukkhattuṃ) as the verse's opening word; confirm the Pali text and Devanagari.
